reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Neurocutaneous Disorders (current reference texts)
clinicalPearls: Defined by the coexistence of a capillary malformation (naevus flammeus) with a pigmentary lesion such as dermal melanocytosis or naevus spilus in the same patient
Reflects twin spotting (didymosis), where two distinct mosaic clones arise from post-zygotic recombination, giving overlapping vascular and pigmentary birthmarks
Somatic activating variants in GNAQ and GNA11 have been implicated, linking it mechanistically to Sturge-Weber and phakomatosis pigmentokeratotica
The current classification groups cases by vascular-plus-pigmentary combination and by the presence or absence of systemic involvement
Extensive facial capillary malformation raises the risk of associated Sturge-Weber syndrome and Klippel-Trenaunay overgrowth
Ocular melanocytosis (naevus of Ota) predisposes to glaucoma and warrants ophthalmological surveillance
Management is generic: pulsed-dye laser for the vascular component, Q-switched laser for pigment, and screening for ocular and neurological complications
reference.pathophysiology: Phakomatosis pigmentovascularis is best understood as an example of twin spotting, in which post-zygotic somatic recombination or independent mosaic variants generate two genetically distinct cell populations that produce adjacent vascular and pigmentary birthmarks. Activating variants in the GNAQ and GNA11 genes, which encode G-protein alpha subunits, have been identified and account for the overlap with other GNAQ-driven conditions such as Sturge-Weber syndrome. The capillary malformation reflects dysregulated vascular development, while the coexisting dermal melanocytosis or naevus spilus reflects abnormal migration and persistence of dermal melanocytes. Where the mosaic clones involve leptomeningeal or ocular tissue, neurological and ocular complications ensue.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian spot, naevus of Ota)
additionalInvestigations: Full skin examination to document vascular and pigmentary components
MRI and MRA of the brain where leptomeningeal involvement or Sturge-Weber is suspected
Ophthalmological assessment including intraocular pressure for ocular melanocytosis and glaucoma
Limb imaging and measurement where overgrowth suggests Klippel-Trenaunay
Skin biopsy in atypical or diagnostically uncertain lesions
Molecular testing of affected tissue for GNAQ/GNA11 variants where available
redFlags: Seizures or focal neurological signs suggesting leptomeningeal angiomatosis
Raised intraocular pressure or visual symptoms from ocular melanocytosis
Progressive limb overgrowth or venous complications
Any change within a melanocytic lesion raising concern for melanoma
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on associated systemic disease; purely cutaneous phakomatosis pigmentovascularis is benign and mainly a cosmetic concern, whereas coexisting Sturge-Weber, glaucoma or Klippel-Trenaunay overgrowth carries the associated morbidity of those conditions.
pitfalls: Treating the birthmarks cosmetically without screening for Sturge-Weber, glaucoma or limb overgrowth
Missing ocular melanocytosis and its lifelong glaucoma risk
Attributing all vascular lesions to a simple port-wine stain and overlooking the pigmentary component
Failing to arrange neuroimaging in extensive facial capillary malformation
references: Happle R. Mosaicism in Human Skin
management: No specific systemic therapy exists, so treatment targets the individual vascular and pigmentary components and any systemic involvement
Pulsed-dye laser treatment of the capillary malformation for cosmetically significant naevus flammeus
Laser therapy for dermal melanocytosis or naevus of Ota as indicated
Ophthalmological surveillance with intraocular pressure monitoring and glaucoma treatment where ocular melanocytosis is present
Neurological assessment with brain MRI and MRA and antiepileptic therapy where Sturge-Weber leptomeningeal involvement is suspected
Assessment and management of Klippel-Trenaunay-type overgrowth with limb imaging, compression and orthopaedic input
Multidisciplinary follow-up across dermatology, ophthalmology and neurology, with genetic counselling noting the sporadic mosaic GNAQ and GNA11 basis
